response: Rust does not have a garbage collector. Rust uses compile-time static analysis through ownership rules to manage memory; Go uses runtime garbage collection. The speed difference: Rust eliminates entire categories of memory errors and avoids GC latency pauses. Go trades memory safety guarantees for simpler runtime behavior.

No. Two disks in the same machine is one failure domain. If the machine dies, both backups go with it. Disaster recovery requires geographically separated copies on different physical infrastructure—a different data center, cloud account, or physical location. Keep one backup offsite.

Regex cannot match arbitrary nesting. Regular expressions are finite-state machines and cannot count or track nesting depth. You can hand-code patterns for fixed nesting levels (explicit for each depth), but true arbitrary-depth nesting requires a parser. If your input has arbitrary parenthesis nesting, switch to a parsing library.

Which is "more accurate" depends on your team's historical track record and your use case. Audit your own retrospectives to see which correlates better to actual delivery before converting.

Lightning strikes the same place repeatedly. The Empire State Building gets hit roughly 20 times per year. A single rod is insufficient for a tall building. You need a grounded conductive system with multiple termination points to safely dissipate current and prevent side flashes to adjacent structures.

Do not publish. Secrets and hard-coded IPs in open source become permanent reconnaissance data for attackers. Once published, credentials live in git history forever even if you delete files. Audit the code, strip all secrets and configuration, test the result, then push.

Compound interest is exponential. If you earn r% per period, your balance multiplies by (1 + r) each period. Repeated multiplication by the same factor is exponential growth. After n periods: balance = P × (1 + r)^n. Linear would add a fixed amount each period. The exponent is what makes it compound.

100% code coverage does not guarantee no bugs. Coverage measures which lines executed in tests, not whether those lines are correct or all edge cases are handled. The final 5% is usually error paths, platform-specific code, or unreachable branches. Reaching it means more lines ran; it doesn't eliminate bugs. Focus on testing critical paths and error cases instead.
